write/ask: Ask a language model for today's weather in Paris, and it is stuck. All it knows is in its weights, and those were fixed when training ended, long before today.
write/prompt: The question is its prompt: the text it is given to continue. And continuing text, one predicted token at a time, is all a language model can do.
write/tool: So the program that runs the model, ordinary code around it, offers it a tool: a function, weather, that looks up a city's forecast. Like a calculator in your hand, a tool does a job its user cannot do well alone.
write/call: To use it, the model writes a call, as text: weather, then Paris in quotes and brackets. The name comes from code, where calling a function means asking it to run, written just like this.
write/markers: Around the call go two marker tokens, call and end call, so the program can find it. Six tokens in all, each predicted like any other.
run/spot: The program reads every token the model writes. When it sees the end marker, it stops the model and reads the call.
run/run: It runs weather of Paris itself, outside the model, and gets back eighteen degrees, sunny.
run/paste: Then it pastes that result into the context, between result markers: five more tokens, written by the program, not the model.
run/resume: And it lets the model write on. With the forecast in view, the next tokens come easily: it is eighteen degrees and sunny.
run/attend: The model reads the result the way it reads any earlier token, through attention. No weight changed: only the context did.
run/steps: Five steps, then. The model writes the call, the program spots it, runs it and pastes the result, and the model writes on.
learn/shots: How does the model know this format? It can pick it up in context: the prompt first shows a solved exchange, with a call, its result and the answer.
learn/new: Then comes the new question, and the likeliest continuation is a call of the same shape.
learn/train: Or it can be trained, with gradient steps, on many transcripts that contain calls, so the format is in its weights. But who writes those, and decides where a call helps?
learn/schick: In 2023, Timo Schick and colleagues at Meta let the model do it. Shown a few examples in its prompt, it proposed calls all through ordinary text, and a program ran each one.
learn/text: Take the sentence: Pittsburgh is also known as the Steel City. One proposed call asks a question-answering tool for Pittsburgh's other name, and gets back Steel City.
learn/other: Another asks which country Pittsburgh is in, and gets back United States.
learn/keep: They kept a call only if its result made the words after it easier to predict: a lower loss on the Steel City. The first call does that, so it stays. The second does not help, so it goes.
learn/tune: Then they trained the model on the text with the kept calls in it, and called it Toolformer. It had taught itself which tool to call, when, and with what inputs.
try/count: Now count. The question took seven tokens, the call six, and the result five: seven plus six plus five is eighteen tokens in view when the model writes on.
try/wrote: Of the final context, the model wrote the call and the answer, six tokens each: twelve. The question came in from outside, and the program wrote the result.
try/p1: Try one: a prompt of twelve tokens, a call of seven, and a result of four. How many tokens are in the context when the model writes on?
try/a1: Twelve plus seven plus four: twenty-three.
